title: Why did Melaka become a crossroads?
essentialQuestion: How can a place on a sea passage bring people together, and what can a later map show or hide?
learningGoal: Explain one way Melaka's location helped trade, and say what a map from 1604 can and cannot show about the earlier Malay sultanate.

warmUp.question: Why might ships stop at a port beside a narrow sea passage?

evidence.question: Which source was made closest in time to the 1400s? Which ones were made much later?

sources.caption: Source 1: UNESCO's description of Melaka and George Town, Historic Cities of the Straits of Malacca (a modern heritage record)
details: Written by UNESCO, a part of the United Nations, for the World Heritage List.
It says the two cities grew through more than 500 years of trade and exchange between East and West in the Strait of Malacca.
It says Melaka shows the early part of this history: the Malay sultanate of the 1400s, then the Portuguese and Dutch periods from the early 1500s.
It names Malay, Chinese and Indian cultures, and three European powers that ruled one after another.
Limit: it is a modern summary about buildings and places. It is not a record made by someone who lived in Melaka in the 1400s.

sources.caption: Source 2: The Government of Malaysia's history page (a modern national summary)
details: It says Melaka's place between East Asia and West Asia helped it become a major trading centre, especially for spices.
It says the Portuguese took Melaka in 1511, the Dutch in 1641, and the British in 1824.
Limit: it is a short modern summary. It does not tell us how each person in Melaka lived.

sources.caption: Source 3: A map of Melaka dated 1604, by the mapmaker Manuel Godinho de Erédia
details: A hand-drawn plan with Portuguese words. It shows a large fort ("Fortaleza"), a river ("Rio de Malaca"), roads and the names of places around the fort.
Limit: it was made about 90 years after the Portuguese took Melaka. It cannot show the city of the Malay sultanate in the 1400s.

sections.heading: A place on a sea passage
sections.text: Melaka is a city on the west coast of the Malay Peninsula, in today's Malaysia. It lies beside the Strait of Malacca, a narrow sea passage between the peninsula and the island of Sumatra. Ships sailing between East Asia and West Asia could pass through it. In the 1400s, Melaka was an important port ruled by a Malay sultanate. A port like this can bring local people, visiting traders, goods and ideas together. Location helps explain why traders stopped there. But geography alone does not tell us who held power, or how each community lived. Find the strait on the modern map before you look at the older map.
sections.simpler: Melaka is a city in Malaysia. It is next to the Strait of Malacca. This strait is a narrow sea between two lands. Ships going between East and West Asia sailed through it. In the 1400s, Melaka was a Malay sultanate. A sultan ruled it. It was a busy port. Traders came with goods and ideas. The strait helps explain why ships stopped there. But it does not tell us who had power.

sections.heading: What a heritage record tells us
sections.text: UNESCO lists Melaka and George Town as World Heritage cities. It says they grew through more than 500 years of trade and exchange between East and West. It names Malay, Chinese and Indian cultures, and three European powers that ruled one after another. In 1511, Portuguese forces took Melaka. Dutch rule began in 1641, and British rule came later. The city changed over these periods. UNESCO's account is a modern heritage summary, not a diary kept by someone in Melaka in the 1400s. It helps us ask questions about long-term change. To hear one resident's view, we would need a source made closer to that person's life.
sections.simpler: UNESCO says Melaka is a heritage city. People today care for its old places. UNESCO says people traded there for more than 500 years. Malay, Chinese and Indian people shaped the city. Europeans ruled it too. In 1511, the Portuguese took Melaka. In 1641, the Dutch took it. Later, the British ruled it. UNESCO wrote this in modern times. It is not a diary from the 1400s.

sections.heading: A map from a later time
sections.text: The second picture is a map of Melaka dated 1604, by a mapmaker named Manuel Godinho de Erédia. It comes from the Portuguese period, about 90 years after the Portuguese took the city. The map shows a large fort, a river and roads, with Portuguese labels. Some places around the fort have names, but we see few homes or people at work. A map shows what its maker chose to show, from his perspective. It is not a photo. So the map can help us study Melaka in the Portuguese period. It cannot show us what the sultanate's city looked like a century before.
sections.simpler: The second picture is an old map. It is dated 1604. That was about 90 years after the Portuguese came. The map shows a big fort and a river. Its words are in Portuguese. We see few homes or workers. A map shows the perspective of the person who drew it. It shows what he chose to draw. So this map tells us about Melaka in 1604. It does not show the city in the 1400s.

checks.question: Which came first: Melaka's Malay sultanate or the map dated 1604?

options.text: The 1604 map was made before the sultanate
options.feedback: Not quite. The sultanate ruled Melaka in the 1400s, long before 1604. Look at the third part of the reading.

options.text: They came at the same time
options.feedback: Not quite. The Portuguese took Melaka in 1511, and the map is from 1604. Check the dates in the reading.
Yes. The sultanate's port was busy in the 1400s. The 1604 map is later evidence, so it cannot show every earlier detail.

checks.question: What is one reason ships and traders came to Melaka?

options.text: It lies beside a busy sea passage
options.feedback: Yes. The Strait of Malacca links East and West Asia. Location helps explain trade, but not who held power.

options.text: It was far away from the sea
options.feedback: Not quite. Melaka is on the coast, beside the strait. Look at the first part of the reading.

options.text: The 1604 map showed ships the way
options.feedback: Not quite. The map was made long after traders first came. Look at the first part of the reading.

write.prompt: In two or three sentences, explain one reason Melaka's location helped trade. Then name one thing the 1604 map cannot show.
selfCheck: I gave one reason about Melaka's location.
I used a detail from the lesson.
I named one thing the 1604 map cannot show.
write.example: Melaka's location helped trade because it lies beside the Strait of Malacca. This is a narrow sea passage. Ships going between East Asia and West Asia could stop at its port. UNESCO says people traded there for more than 500 years. The 1604 map can help us learn about Melaka when the Portuguese ruled it. But it cannot show the city as it was when a sultan ruled it, in the 1400s.

speak.partnerTask: With a partner, compare the modern map and the 1604 map. Say one thing each map shows that the other does not.
speak.independentTask: Say or write a short comparison: one thing the modern map shows, and one thing the 1604 map shows.

watch.title: Melaka and George Town, Historic Cities of the Straits ... (UNESCO/NHK)
watch.why: It is UNESCO's own short film about Melaka's heritage city, which has buildings from several periods of its long trading history.
watch.beforeQuestion: What do you think could make a port a meeting place for many different people?
watch.afterQuestion: Choose one building or place in the film. Which period does the film link it to: the sultanate, Portuguese, Dutch or British?
watch.summary: This is a short film by UNESCO and NHK, a TV company in Japan. It is about Melaka and George Town, two old cities by the Strait of Malacca. UNESCO's notes on the film say that people traded in the two cities for more than 500 years. Goods and ideas moved between East and West. People from Asia and Europe shaped the cities and left a mixed heritage. The notes say Melaka's old buildings show the early part of this history. UNESCO says this history began with the Malay sultanate in the 1400s. Then the Portuguese and the Dutch ruled, from the early 1500s. As you watch, remember that the film was made in our time. It shows buildings that are still standing, not people from the 1400s.
keyPoints: UNESCO says Melaka and George Town grew through more than 500 years of trade.
Melaka's history began with the Malay sultanate in the 1400s; Portuguese and Dutch rule came later.
A film made today shows buildings that survive, not daily life in the 1400s.

visual.description: A modern explanatory map, with the words "modern map, not a map from the 1400s" in one corner. Main panel: the southern Malay Peninsula and the east coast of Sumatra, with the narrow Strait of Malacca between them, labelled "Strait of Malacca". A dot on the peninsula's west coast labelled "Melaka". Two broad, soft arrows at the ends of the strait, one labelled "to and from East Asia" (pointing toward the South China Sea) and one "to and from West Asia" (pointing toward the Indian Ocean), drawn as general directions, not ship routes. Under the map, an uncluttered strip of four boxes left to right: "1400s: Malay sultanate", "from 1511: Portuguese", "from 1641: Dutch", "from 1824: British", with a small marker on the Portuguese box reading "1604 map made here". No flags, ships, people or invented old-style decoration.
visual.alt: A modern map of the narrow Strait of Malacca between the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra, with Melaka marked on the peninsula's coast and arrows showing the ways to East Asia and West Asia. Below, a timeline shows the Malay sultanate in the 1400s, then Portuguese rule from 1511, Dutch from 1641 and British from 1824, with the 1604 map in the Portuguese period.
visual.caption: A modern map made for this lesson, not a map from the 1400s. The timeline shows that the 1604 map belongs to the Portuguese period.
visual.lookClosely: How could the strait help connect travellers from far away?

secondVisual.description: Wikimedia Commons file "Portuguese Malacca map.png": a black-and-white reproduction of a hand-drawn plan of Melaka by Manuel Godinho de Erédia (the file page spells it Herédia), dated 1604 on the file page, which credits it to his "Declaraçam de Malaca e da India Meridional com Cathay". Its title reads "Planta da cidade e povoaçoens de Malaca" (plan of the city and settlements of Melaka). It shows a large walled fort labelled "Fortaleza" beside the river "Rio de Malaca", roads, a compass rose, and Portuguese labels naming settlements around the fort. The file page marks the reproduction CC0. Chosen because it is a real source from the Portuguese period, so learners can practise placing a source in time and asking whose lives it leaves out.
secondVisual.alt: A black-and-white hand-drawn map of Melaka. A large walled fort labelled Fortaleza sits beside a winding river labelled Rio de Malaca. Roads lead out to places named in Portuguese, and a compass rose and long straight lines cross the sea at the bottom.
secondVisual.caption: A map of Melaka, dated 1604, from the time of Portuguese rule. It was made about 90 years after 1511, so it cannot show the city of the 1400s.
secondVisual.lookClosely: Which features did the mapmaker draw in most detail? Whose lives are hard to see?

sensitiveNotes: The Portuguese conquest of Melaka in 1511 and the Dutch takeover in 1641 involved fighting; British rule came through a treaty in 1824. The lesson states these changes of rule plainly and without battle detail; keep it that way. Never ask learners about their own or their family's history, home country, religion or ethnicity; when they think about residents' views, they name sources to look for, not personal stories.
educatorNotes: Aim: learners explain how Melaka's place on a sea passage helped trade, and name a clear limit of a later map. Evidence move: point to the date 1604 on the map and its caption before asking anything about the 15th-century sultanate. A sound answer says location helps explain a port, and that the later map has an explicit limit. Misconception to address: the map was not drawn during the sultanate, and a modern UNESCO summary and a 1604 map are two different kinds of source.

Source caveats: Melaka was one of many ports in the region, so avoid suggesting it stands for all of Southeast Asia; and peoples named in a heritage summary did not share equal power. The date 1604 comes from the Commons file page and the brief. Erédia's book named in the file's credit line, the Declaraçam de Malaca, is usually dated about 1613; an NUS Press study says one of his strait maps in it is dated 1604 but does not date this city plan. Either way the map is from the Portuguese period, long after 1511.
